tour.title: Sultanahmet: From the Hippodrome to the Golden Horn
tour.summary: Fourteen stops through Byzantine and Ottoman Istanbul, from the Hippodrome to the Eminönü ferry piers.
tour.overviewText:
Welcome to Istanbul, the only great city that sits on two continents at once. This entire walk stays on the European side, on a small peninsula that reaches out into the water where the Golden Horn meets the Bosphorus and the Sea of Marmara. For a thousand years this was Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire. For another four and a half centuries it was the seat of the Ottoman sultans. Layer has been piled on layer and almost nothing has been cleared away, which is exactly what makes the place extraordinary.

The route covers about three and a half kilometres and fourteen stops, and it will take most of a day if you go inside everything. It begins on Sultanahmet Square, once the Hippodrome, a Roman chariot-racing track where tens of thousands of spectators roared at the Blues and the Greens. Three monuments still stand on its central spine. From there the walk moves through the great mosques, down into an underground cistern, along a restored Ottoman lane, into a park where Ottoman law was changed, and finally downhill through a working neighbourhood to the ferry piers at Eminönü.

A few practical things before you set off. Turkish museum prices change frequently, sometimes more than once a year, so treat every figure in this app as a guide and always check at the gate. Two stops here are working mosques and both close to visitors during the five daily prayers, with a longer closure at Hagia Sophia on Fridays around midday. Dress modestly: shoulders and knees covered, and women should carry a headscarf. Bring cash for small purchases and for tea.

Start early. By half past eight the square is quiet, the light is soft, and the monuments are more or less yours. Wear comfortable shoes, expect cobbles, and do not try to see everything in a single day if you would rather enjoy it. Ready? Let us begin at the obelisk.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Almost entirely flat and much of it pedestrianised, with one gentle climb to the palace courtyard and a downhill stretch to the water. Cobbles and uneven paving throughout, and roughly three and a half kilometres of walking spread across the day.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start between 08:30 and 09:00, when Sultanahmet Square and the Blue Mosque are quiet. Avoid Hagia Sophia on Friday around midday, when it closes for congregational prayer. Finish at Eminönü in the late afternoon, when the light on the Golden Horn is at its best.

stops.name: Obelisk of Theodosius
stops.narration:
Look up. That granite needle has been standing here for more than fifteen hundred years, but it was already ancient when it arrived. The Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose the Third raised it at Karnak around fourteen fifty B C. The Romans shipped it down the Nile and across the sea to Constantinople, and in the year three ninety the emperor Theodosius had it hoisted onto the spine of the Hippodrome. The lifting went wrong. The obelisk cracked, and what survives is only the upper section, about nineteen metres of granite, raised to nearly twenty-six by its marble base. 

Look at that base. It is carved with the emperor and his court watching the chariot races from their box, and in one corner a water organ is being played. Imagine this long oval packed with tens of thousands of people, screaming for the Blues and the Greens. The bronze cubes wedged under each corner are the original lifting gear. After sixteen centuries they are still holding it up.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Public square, no ticket. Prices for Istanbul's ticketed sites change frequently, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Open access, 24 hours. Best in daylight.
stops.accessibility: Level paved square with tactile paving; the monument itself is fenced. Good step-free access from the tram stop at Sultanahmet.
stops.insiderTip: The pedestal reliefs are the real prize and most people photograph only the obelisk. Walk right round the base: the south face shows a chariot race in progress, the east face shows the emperor handing out the victor's crown, with the water organ at the bottom right.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn and walk south along the middle of the square, keeping the obelisk behind you. After about thirty metres you will come to a short, twisted bronze column on a stone base. That is your next stop.
stops.photoSearch: Obelisk of Thutmosis III, Istanbul, Turkey 001.jpg

stops.name: Serpentine Column (Plataean Tripod)
stops.narration: It looks like a stub, and that is the whole point. This twisted bronze stump is the oldest man-made object in Istanbul, and it was never meant to be looked at. In four seventy-nine B C, thirty-one Greek city-states beat the Persian army at Plataea. They melted down the spoils, cast three snakes twined into one column, and set a golden tripod on their heads at Delphi. Herodotus mentions it by name. For eight hundred years it stood at the sanctuary of Apollo. Then Constantine the Great carried it off to his new capital as a trophy. The golden tripod vanished long ago, and the three serpent heads were smashed off around seventeen hundred. One of them survives, and it is in the Archaeology Museum a few minutes' walk from here. Run your eyes over the coils. You can still make out the names of the Greek cities cut into the metal. It is a war memorial that outlasted the empire that won the war.
stops.accessibility: Level paved ground, low base, easy to approach in a wheelchair.
stops.insiderTip: The surviving serpent head in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums is easy to miss: ask for the Serpent Column head in the Ancient Orient section rather than hunting for it. The lower jaw is broken off, which is why it reads as a snake rather than the original three-headed form.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue south another thirty metres or so. You are heading for the tall, rough stone obelisk at the far end of the line. It is the plainest of the three monuments, and you will see it immediately.

stops.name: Obelisk of Constantine (Walled Obelisk)
stops.narration:
This one is the odd one out. Unlike its neighbours it is not Egyptian, not Greek, and not even a true obelisk. It is rough masonry stacked into an obelisk shape, probably in the fourth or fifth century, built to mirror the granite one nearby, because a proper Roman circus was supposed to have two. For a while it was the most dazzling object on the square. In the tenth century the emperor Constantine the Seventh had it sheathed in gilded bronze plaques showing the victories of his grandfather, and a Greek poem was carved on the base boasting that this bronze was now the wonder of the world, just as the Colossus had been at Rhodes. In twelve oh four, crusaders tore the gold off and melted it into coin. Later, Ottoman trainee soldiers used the monument as a climbing wall, which is why the stonework looks so battered. 

Look closely at the surface. The plaster is studded with fragments of broken pottery, and locals once swore they cracked to warn the city of high winds.
stops.accessibility: Level paved ground. The base is unfenced, so approach with care in low light.
stops.insiderTip: Stand a few paces back and compare the three monuments side by side. The Walled Obelisk is the only one built to be an obelisk rather than being one, which explains why it has aged so badly next to two pieces of solid granite.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn right and walk north back along the square, about two hundred and fifty metres. You are retracing the line of the old race track. At the far northern end, near the tram line, you will find an ornate domed fountain. That is the next stop.

stops.name: German Fountain (Alman Çeşmesi)
stops.narration: An octagonal gazebo, a bronze dome, golden mosaics inside, and a German inscription on the side. This fountain is a diplomatic gift, and it stands on ground with a darker history. Kaiser Wilhelm the Second visited Istanbul in eighteen ninety-eight, partly to win Ottoman approval for a railway running from Berlin to Baghdad. Sultan Abdul Hamid the Second was grateful, so Germany built this fountain in pieces, shipped them out, and assembled it here in nineteen oh one. Look up under the dome and you will find two monograms repeated eight times: the sultan's calligraphic signature and the Kaiser's letter W beneath a crown. On the bronze band, in German, Wilhelm dedicates the fountain to the memory of his visit. Long before any of that, this was the site of a plane tree known as the Vakvak Tree. In sixteen fifty-six, rebellious soldiers strung the bodies of senior officials from its branches. It became known as the Bloody Plane. A cheerful little fountain with a violent address.
stops.openingHours: Open access, 24 hours. The water has not run for years; it is a monument, not a working fountain.
stops.accessibility: Level paved square, step-free from the tram line. The fountain has a raised base with steps, but it is fully visible from ground level.
stops.insiderTip: Step inside and look straight up. The ceiling mosaics are gold and almost nobody looks. The eight medallions alternate between Abdülhamid's tughra on green and Wilhelm's crowned W on Prussian blue.
stops.nextStopDirections: Face south and walk about two hundred metres across the square. The huge mosque with six minarets and a cascade of domes will be ahead of you and slightly to your left. Cross towards its main courtyard.

stops.name: Blue Mosque (Sultan Ahmed Mosque)
stops.narration: Ahmed the First was nineteen when he began this mosque, and he was determined to outdo everyone. The result has six minarets, which caused an uproar, because Mecca's sacred mosque had six as well and the sultan stood accused of claiming equality with the holy city. His solution was to pay for a seventh minaret in Mecca. Inside are more than twenty thousand hand-made tiles from Iznik, and it is those tiles, blue and turquoise, that gave the building its English nickname. The sultan was not only ambitious, he was unusual. He insisted on working on the site with his own hands, and he paid the workmen from his personal purse rather than the treasury. He died at twenty-seven, within months of the mosque being finished, and he is buried just outside the wall you are facing. As you go in, remember this is a working mosque, not a museum. Shoes off, shoulders and knees covered, hair covered for women, voices low. There is no ticket and no entry charge.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free for worshippers and for tourists. No ticket and no booking. Donations are not requested at the door; ignore anyone offering to sell you entry.
stops.openingHours: Generally open to visitors from about 08:30 until around dusk, but closed to tourists during each of the five daily prayers, roughly 60 to 90 minutes each time. On Fridays the mosque is closed to visitors until about 14:30. Prayer times shift daily, so check the day's timetable.
stops.accessibility: Step-free through the courtyard, but the prayer hall has a raised threshold and thick carpets; a small ramp is usually available. Wheelchairs can enter the visitor section. Women are asked to cover their heads; scarves are lent free at the door.
stops.insiderTip: Go to the visitors' entrance on the south side rather than queueing at the main courtyard gate. Late afternoon, roughly an hour before the sunset prayer, gives the softest light through the stained glass and the smallest crowd.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the mosque by the north side and walk north-east across Ayasofya Square, about three hundred metres, keeping the domes of Hagia Sophia on your right. Between the Blue Mosque and Hagia Sophia you will pass a long stone building with two rows of small domes and tall chimneys. Stop at its main door on the square.

stops.name: Ayasofya Haseki Hürrem Sultan Baths
stops.narration:
Between the two great mosques sits a bathhouse, and behind it lies one of the great power stories of the sixteenth century. Hürrem Sultan, whose name is said hoo-REM, was taken from what is now Ukraine, brought to the imperial palace as a slave, and rose to become the legal wife of Suleiman the Magnificent. That was unprecedented for an Ottoman sultan. She was clever, ambitious and ruthless, and European ambassadors called her Roxelana. In fifteen fifty-six she commissioned this building from Mimar Sinan, the empire's greatest architect, and he placed it on the site of the ancient Baths of Zeuxippus, right on the axis between Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque, so bathers arriving from either direction could stop for a wash. What makes it unusual is the plan: two complete, symmetrical bathhouses, one for men and one for women, set end to end on a single line. Sinan had never done that before. 

It served bathers for centuries, spent decades as a carpet showroom, and reopened in twenty eleven after a long restoration.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Not a museum: this is a working luxury hammam, priced in euros. Packages run 110 EUR for 45 minutes, 155 EUR for 60 minutes, 220 EUR for 80 minutes and 300 EUR for 110 minutes. That is roughly 6,100 TL to 16,600 TL at an exchange rate of about 55 TL to the euro, but the lira figure moves with the currency, so treat it as a guide and verify with the operator.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 07:00 to 24:00 in summer and 08:00 to 22:00 in winter. Reservations are strongly advised, particularly for evening slots.
stops.accessibility: Ground-floor entrance from Ayasofya Square with a small step; the historic interior has wet marble floors and low thresholds, so assistance is advisable. Tell staff in advance if you need step-free access or a seated treatment.
stops.insiderTip: You do not have to book a treatment to see the best of it. The monumental entrance on the square, with its green ground, red and white palmettes and gold inscription, is free to look at, and the twin lead-covered domes behind are clearest from the corner of Ayasofya Square in late afternoon.
stops.nextStopDirections: With your back to the hammam, walk west along Yerebatan Street for about one hundred and fifty metres. Look on your left for a plain doorway with a small sign and a short flight of steps going down. That is the entrance to the cistern.

stops.name: Basilica Cistern (Yerebatan Sarnıcı)
stops.narration:
Down a plain staircase, out of the noise and the heat, is a cathedral made of water. Justinian built this in the sixth century to hold the city's drinking water, and it is enormous: about one hundred and forty metres long, held up by three hundred and thirty-six marble columns, most of them salvaged from older pagan temples. Thousands of enslaved people worked on it. By the sixteenth century it had been forgotten by almost everyone except the locals, who lowered buckets through holes in their floors and sometimes caught fish. A French scholar named Petrus Gyllius found it in fifteen sixty-five and was rowed between the columns by lamplight, watching fish swim under the boat. 

Look for the column carved with tear-shaped patterns, then walk to the far end. Two blocks there are carved with the face of Medusa, one upside down and one on its side. Nobody knows why. The usual guess is that a Christian builder, reusing a pagan image, turned it over so it could not cast a spell.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Foreign adult daytime ticket 1,950 TL, confirmed in an official Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality notice dated 3 February 2026. Turkish citizens pay 450 TL, discounted 90 TL. Evening sessions, 19:30 to 22:00, cost 3,000 TL for foreign visitors. Children under seven go free. Museum prices in Turkey change often, so verify before you travel.
stops.openingHours: Open daily. Daytime visits run roughly 09:00 to 18:30, with a separate evening session from 19:30 to 22:00. Queues peak between 10:00 and 15:00, and the ticket price is higher at night.
stops.accessibility: Lifts and ramps have been added since the 2020 to 2022 restoration, but the route is a one-way steel walkway over water with low lighting and some uneven thresholds. Wheelchair users should ask staff at the entrance, as the accessible route may be guided.
stops.insiderTip: Book a timed slot online and go straight to opening time or to the evening session. The lighting is far better after dark, and the crowds thin dramatically. The Medusa heads are at the far, north-west end, and most visitors turn back before reaching them.
stops.nextStopDirections: Climb back up to street level, turn right, and walk east along Yerebatan Street for about one hundred and fifty metres until the road opens into a square. The great domed building ahead of you is Hagia Sophia. Walk to the far end of the square and look for the visitors' gate on the north-east side, next to the outer gate of Topkapı Palace.
stops.photoSearch: Cisterna Basílica, Estambul, Turquía, 2024-09-28, DD 58-60 HDR.jpg

stops.name: Hagia Sophia Mosque (Ayasofya)
stops.narration:
For nearly a thousand years this was the largest cathedral on earth, and when Justinian opened it in five thirty-seven he is said to have cried out that he had outdone Solomon. He had a point. The dome is about thirty-one metres across and appears to float, because the builders hid its enormous weight in a cascade of half-domes. Twice the church was wrecked by riot and fire, and twice it was rebuilt. In fourteen fifty-three Mehmed the Second rode in and turned it into a mosque, adding minarets and plastering over the mosaics. In nineteen thirty-five it became a museum. In twenty twenty it became a mosque again. That is five identities in fifteen centuries. Non-Muslim visitors now enter by a separate gate and pay a fee to walk the upper gallery; the ground floor belongs to worshippers. 

Upstairs, look for the Deesis mosaic, with Christ flanked by the Virgin and John the Baptist. Then find the balustrade in the south gallery, where a Viking of the imperial guard scratched his name in runes a thousand years ago.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Foreign visitors pay about 25 EUR for the upper-gallery tourist route. The fee is set in euros rather than lira, so the lira equivalent moves daily; at roughly 55 TL to the euro that is about 1,380 TL, but verify the day's rate. Turkish citizens pay a much lower lira rate, and worshippers entering to pray are never charged. Children under eight enter free with a passport. Istanbul museum passes no longer cover Hagia Sophia.
stops.openingHours: Open to tourists daily, generally 09:00 to 19:30, opening at 08:00 from April to September. Closed to visitors during all five daily prayers. On Fridays the closure is longest, roughly 12:00 to 14:30, for the weekly congregational prayer. Last entry is well before closing, so do not arrive late.
stops.accessibility: There is a step-free visitors' gate with security screening, and the ground-floor route is level, but the upper gallery is reached by a steep stone ramp with no lift. Visitors who cannot manage the ramp can view the ground floor. Wheelchairs are available on request at the gate.
stops.insiderTip: The tourist entrance is not the grand door facing Sultanahmet Square. It is on the north-east side, beside the outer gate of Topkapı Palace, opposite the Sultan Ahmed the Third fountain. Security can take ten minutes early and half an hour at peak times, so arrive before opening.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk east for about one hundred and twenty metres, past the Sultan Ahmed the Third fountain on your left, to the great stone gateway in the wall. That is the Imperial Gate, the main entrance to the palace. Buy your ticket just inside the first courtyard rather than at the gate.
stops.photoSearch: Istanbul Türkiye Hagia Sophia Grand Mosque Ank Kumar Infosys Limited 01.jpg

stops.name: Topkapı Palace Museum (Topkapı Sarayı)
stops.narration:
Through that gate is not a palace so much as a small walled town, and for four centuries it ran an empire. Mehmed the Second began building in the fourteen sixties, and sultans lived here until the eighteen fifties, when they moved across the water to a new palace on the Bosphorus. The layout is a deliberate hierarchy of four courtyards, each more private than the last. The first was open to the public. In the second stood the treasury and the divan, the imperial council, and the sultan could listen to his own ministers through a grilled window nicknamed the Eye of the Sultan, entirely unseen. The third holds the throne room and the treasury. The fourth is the sultan's private garden, with a view straight up the Bosphorus. 

Do not skip the Harem, which needs its own ticket. It is a maze of corridors and courtyards where the sultan's mother, the Valide Sultan, frequently wielded more real power than her son. And note the closing day: the palace shuts on Tuesdays.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Combined ticket covering palace, Harem and Hagia Irene: 2,750 TL for foreign visitors. Bought separately, the Harem is 1,050 TL and Hagia Irene 1,050 TL, so the combined ticket is better value. Turkish citizens pay 500 TL. Free for under sixes, and 100 TL for Turkish students. These figures come from a well-maintained independent visitor guide rather than the ministry's own site, so treat them as a strong indication and verify at the gate; Turkish museum prices rise frequently.
stops.openingHours: Open daily except Tuesday, 09:00 to 18:00, with the ticket office closing at 17:00. Closed on the first day of Ramadan Bayram and on 1 January. Open on 23 April, 1 May and 29 October. Last entry to the Harem is earlier than the palace closing time.
stops.accessibility: The first and second courtyards are largely step-free and paved, but the Harem, the third courtyard and the pavilions involve thresholds, narrow doorways and uneven cobbles. A wheelchair route exists but is limited. Allow plenty of time; distances inside the walls are much greater than they look.
stops.insiderTip: Arrive at opening. By ten o'clock the queue at the Imperial Gate can run the length of the courtyard. Go straight to the Harem first while the palace proper is still filling up, then work back through the treasury and the Baghdad Kiosk, which has the best Bosphorus view in the complex.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the Imperial Gate and turn left, then immediately left again into the narrow lane that runs alongside the palace wall. Walk about one hundred metres; you are now in a street of restored timber houses. Take your time.
stops.photoSearch: The Gate of Felicity (Bâbüssaâde), Topkapi Palace, Istanbul, Turkey.jpg

stops.name: Soğukçeşme Street (Soğukçeşme Sokağı)
stops.narration:
This short lane is the prettiest street in Sultanahmet and almost nobody notices it. It is squeezed between the walls of Hagia Sophia and Topkapı Palace, and its name means Cold Fountain Street, after a fountain at the end nearest the park. In the nineteen eighties it was a run-down strip of workshops and sheds. Then a conservation campaign rebuilt the Ottoman houses here, recreating the timber frames and the upper floors that lean out over the pavement. That overhang was not decoration. It shaded the walkway below and let neighbours lean out and talk across the street, which is how Ottoman lanes were designed to work. 

Here is the honest detail: the houses are actually reinforced concrete faced with wood, not original timber, so this is a careful reconstruction rather than a survival. Nine of them form a hotel now, each named after the shrub beside it. Jasmine House, Wisteria House, Honeysuckle House. Two are cafés. Come early and you will have the whole lane to yourself.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public street. The cafés and the hotel are private businesses.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times as a public street, though the cafés keep normal daytime hours and the lane is loveliest in daylight.
stops.accessibility: Pedestrianised and car-free, but the surface is cobbled and slightly sloping, with a gentle rise towards the palace gate. Manageable in a wheelchair with care; there are no steps along the street itself.
stops.insiderTip: One of the houses holds the İstanbul Kitaplığı, a library of more than ten thousand books about the city, and Turkey's sixth president, Fahri Korutürk, was born in this street. At the Gülhane end, a Byzantine cistern under the lane now houses a restaurant, which is a good excuse to look at the vaulting.
stops.nextStopDirections: Follow the lane north to its end, then turn left onto the main road and walk about two hundred metres uphill. The entrance to the park is on your right, marked by a small pavilion jutting out over the pavement. Go through the gate.

stops.name: Gülhane Park (Gülhane Parkı)
stops.narration:
This was the private outer garden of the palace: roses, tulips, cypresses, and a wall to keep ordinary people out. Then, in eighteen thirty-nine, a different kind of event happened here. The young sultan Abdulmecid gathered the empire's leading men in the park and had a decree read aloud. It promised security of life and property for all subjects, fair taxation, and an end to arbitrary execution. It is remembered as the Decree of Gülhane, and it is usually treated as the opening of the great era of Ottoman reform. Nothing changed overnight and the promises were only partly kept, but a sultan had publicly declared that he ruled under law. Today the park is free and full of plane trees and pigeons, and every April it turns scarlet and yellow for the city's tulip festival. 

Follow the path uphill past the little pavilion where the sultan once watched processions go by, and the view opens out towards the water.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free admission to the park. The small Museum of the History of Science and Technology in Islam, inside the park, charges its own separate modest ticket.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, broadly dawn until late evening; most sources quote around 06:00 to 22:00 in summer with shorter hours in winter. Hours vary with the season, so verify at the gate.
stops.accessibility: Main paths are wide, paved and gently sloping, with benches at intervals, so the park is among the easiest stops on this walk. Some side paths and the upper terraces have steps and no handrails.
stops.insiderTip: Most people enter from the waterfront side. Coming in from the palace end, as you are, means you walk the park in reverse and reach the Alay Köşkü before the crowds. The tea garden halfway down is cheap and has proper çay in tulip glasses.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the park by the main gate, cross to the other side of the road and walk downhill with the tram tracks, heading towards the water. After about four hundred metres, where the road bends and the grand old railway station comes into view on your right, you are in the Hoca Paşa district. Stop near the station forecourt.

stops.name: Hoca Paşa
stops.narration:
You have crossed out of the museum district and into a quarter where people actually live and work. This quarter is named after Hoja Pasha, a fifteenth-century scholar and military judge who served Mehmed the Second. It is the sort of place visitors walk through without seeing: hardware shops, tailors, a small mosque, and a dense grid of modest hotels. The landmark is Sirkeci Station, a couple of minutes north. Opened in eighteen ninety, it was the last stop on the Orient Express, the train that carried aristocrats, spies, exiles and Agatha Christie's characters into the Ottoman capital. The station was built as a gateway to an empire, and it still has a whiff of that about it. 

If you are hungry, this is the moment to step off the route. The streets around Hoca Paşa are full of plain, cheap lokantas serving soup, beans and grilled meat to office workers and taxi drivers rather than to tour groups. Look for the ones with no menu in English.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Public neighbourhood, no ticket. Expect to pay for food and drink only.
stops.openingHours: Always open. The station is accessible during rail operating hours; the surrounding streets are liveliest on weekday mornings.
stops.accessibility: Pavements here are narrow, often obstructed and sometimes stepped, and kerbs are high, so this is the least accessible stretch of the walk. Sirkeci Station itself has step-free access to the main hall.
stops.insiderTip: Sirkeci Station has a small museum and restaurant in the old Orient Express departure hall, and the 1890 building is worth ten minutes even if you are not catching a train. The station also connects to the Marmaray tunnel under the Bosphorus, which is the fastest way back if you decide to stop here.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the station forecourt walk west, away from the water, for about five hundred metres. Follow the crowds and the smell of roasting coffee. The street narrows and the shopfronts fill with sacks of spices and pyramids of Turkish delight. The arched gateway ahead is the Egyptian Bazaar.
stops.photoSearch: Estación de Sirkeci, Estambul, Turquía, 2024-09-28, DD 76-78 HDR.jpg

stops.name: Egyptian Bazaar (Mısır Çarşısı)
stops.narration: You smell it before you see it. Cumin, sumac, dried mint, cinnamon and saffron spill out of the doorways, and underneath them is the dark, roasted smell of coffee ground on the spot. This is the Egyptian Bazaar, finished in the sixteen sixties as part of the New Mosque complex beside it. The name has nothing to do with the goods. It comes from the Egyptian tax revenues that paid for the building. It is an L-shaped arcade of about ninety vaulted shops, and it was designed to be walked through in a few minutes rather than to swallow you whole the way the Grand Bazaar does. Two rules. First, taste everything you are offered. It is normal, it is free, and it is how business is done. Second, never take the first price. Open at about half, and expect to settle near two thirds. And if anyone offers you saffron for a couple of euros, walk on. Real saffron costs many times that.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter; you pay only for what you buy. Bargaining is expected, and opening prices are often a third to a half above what a seller will accept.
stops.openingHours: Open every day including Sunday, roughly 08:00 to 19:30 Monday to Saturday and from about 09:30 on Sundays. Closed on the main days of Ramadan Bayram and Kurban Bayram. Note that the Grand Bazaar, unlike this one, shuts all day Sunday.
stops.accessibility: Mostly level with a smooth stone floor, but the aisles are narrow and crowded and the two main gates have a small threshold. Not step-free throughout, and hard to navigate in a wheelchair at busy times.
stops.insiderTip: Ignore the main Eminönü gate and use the quieter Mahmutpaşa entrance at the other end, which connects uphill towards the Grand Bazaar. And leave by the coffee shop on Tahmis Street, where Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi has been roasting beans since 1871; the queue outside is the local benchmark for good Turkish coffee.
stops.nextStopDirections: Exit through the Eminönü gate, beside the New Mosque, and walk the short distance north to the water. Cross the tram tracks carefully and you are on the quay. You have reached Eminönü, and this is where the walk ends.
stops.photoSearch: PXL 20241211 081724127.MP Egyptian Bazaar Mısır Çarşısı Spice Bazar Istanbul, Turkiye 03.jpg

stops.name: Eminönü
stops.narration:
You have arrived at the water. This is Eminönü, where the city meets the Golden Horn, and it has been a landing place for two thousand years. Behind you stands the New Mosque with its arcade of shops, and the bazaar you just left. In front of you, ferries slide out towards Üsküdar and Kadıköy on the Asian side. To your right is the Galata Bridge, lined with men holding fishing rods, and beneath it a row of restaurants serving fried fish in bread. Look across the water and you can pick out the Galata Tower on the skyline. This is also the busiest transport hub in the old city: tram, ferry, bus and the Marmaray tunnel under the Bosphorus all meet within a few minutes' walk of where you are standing. 

The classic Istanbul meal is right here. Buy a balik ekmek, a grilled mackerel sandwich, from one of the bobbing boats at the quay, sit on a bollard, and eat it while the ferries come and go. That is the tour finished. Stay a while.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Public waterfront, no ticket. Ferries, food and the Galata Bridge are all pay-as-you-go. An Istanbulkart is the cheapest way to travel onward.
stops.openingHours: Always open. Ferries run from roughly 06:30 to 21:00 with frequent departures; the fish boats and bridge restaurants operate through the day and into the evening.
stops.accessibility: The quay is broad and level with dropped kerbs, and the piers have ramps, though boarding a ferry can involve a gap and a moving deck; staff will assist if asked. The Galata Bridge has a level pedestrian walkway.
stops.insiderTip: Walk up onto the Galata Bridge and take the lower level back. The upper deck is for fishing and photographs, while the lower deck is a continuous arcade of fish restaurants. From the middle of the bridge you get the postcard view back towards the New Mosque and the Topkapı headland.
stops.nextStopDirections: The tour ends here at the Eminönü ferry piers and the southern landing of the Galata Bridge. From this point you can catch a ferry to Üsküdar or Kadıköy, walk across the bridge to Galata and Beyoğlu, or take the T1 tram back up the hill to Sultanahmet. Whichever you choose, allow a few minutes to stand at the rail and watch the light on the water.
